title: What Estate Sale Dealers Grab First — Before You Even Open the Door
description:
Forty years I ran estate sales in Ohio, and I've watched the same dealers walk past the good china and go straight for the same few things. This is what they grab first, how you spot each one in ten seconds, what it really sells for (sold listings, not wishful asking prices), and where you can sell it yourself so the money stays in your family.

THE 8 THINGS DEALERS GRAB FIRST
1. Fountain pens (desk drawer) — arrow clip = often Parker, white dot = Sheaffer, nib stamped 14K = real gold. Unrestored Parker 51s usually sell for $40–$100. Sell on eBay (check SOLD) or at a pen show.
2. Signed costume jewelry (top dresser drawer) — turn every pin over: Trifari, Weiss, Coro, Eisenberg, Miriam Haskell. Most signed pieces sell $20–$80; good Haskell or Eisenberg $100–$300. Carved Bakelite bangles: $50–$200. Sell piece by piece, never the whole box.
3. Gold hiding in the junk — broken chains, single earrings, class rings. Look for 10K/14K/18K or 417/585/750; GF, 1/20 or RGP means gold filled/plated. Magnet test: gold never jumps to a magnet. Weigh it in grams, call three buyers (jeweler, coin shop, refiner) and ask what percent of spot they pay — good buyers pay around 80–90%.
4. Sterling silver (the china cabinet) — "sterling" or "925" = solid silver; EPNS or "quadruple plate" = silverplate. Plain sterling creamers usually sell $150–$300; the plated one $5–$15. "Weighted" pieces are mostly filler. Coin shops/metals buyers: a fair one pays about 70–85% of melt.
5. The watch that doesn't run — Hamilton, Elgin, Bulova, Waltham, Longines. Gold-filled Hamiltons/Elgins that don't run often sell $55–$150; solid 14K cases are worth at least their gold. Ask a local watch repair shop before you scrap anything. Railroad pocket watches (21+ jewels) have their own collectors.
6. The paper families throw in the dumpster — real photo postcards (AZO, Velox, Kodak on the back) of small-town Main Streets and depots often sell $40–$200. Old letters, postmarks and church cookbooks sell too. Sell one card at a time with the town name in the title; call your county historical society first.
7. Old Pyrex (kitchen) — all-caps PYREX = vintage Corning. Butterprint, Pink Daisy, Gooseberry. Single Butterprint bowls usually $30–$75, matched nesting sets $200–$300+. Dishwasher-faded = about $10. Sell locally or in Pyrex groups, and keep the set together.
8. Basement hand tools — Stanley planes ($30–$80 for a common No. 4), Bed Rock planes ($100–$300), Disston saws, Keen Kutter, maker-stamped chisels. Don't scrub, paint or grind the rust. Sell on eBay, to tool collectors' clubs or woodworking groups.

WHAT USUALLY ISN'T WORTH IT: full sets of wedding china, common figurines, collector plates with certificates, unmarked cut-glass stemware, encyclopedia sets.

HAZEL'S RULE: never sell on day one. Take anything you're unsure about off the table, and check eBay SOLD items — asking prices are dreams, sold prices are real.

pinned_comment:
What dealers grab first, in one list:
1 Fountain pens (gold nib = 14K) · 2 Signed costume jewelry (Trifari, Weiss, Haskell, Eisenberg) · 3 Gold in the broken jewelry (10K/14K/585 — weigh it, ask % of spot) · 4 Sterling silver ("sterling"/925, not EPNS) · 5 Watches that don't run · 6 Real photo postcards & old paper · 7 Old Pyrex (all-caps stamp, keep the set) · 8 Stanley/Bed Rock planes & old tools.
Never sell on day one — check SOLD listings.
What's the oldest thing in your china cabinet? — Hazel
